# Multiple regression, adjustment, and transformations {#sec-linear-regression-multiple}

```{r}
#| include: false

library(ggplot2)
library(here)

Plot_theme <- source("functions/plot_theme.R")
Plot_theme <- Plot_theme$value

cell_data <- read.csv(here("project/AnalysisData/Cells_Gfap-Pdgfrb.csv"))
cell_data$DPI <- as.numeric(cell_data$DPI)
```

@sec-linear-regression-single-continuous ended with a model we could name precisely and a question we hadn't answered: what happens once we bring a second predictor into it? I've been looking forward to this one, partly because the honest answer turned out to be more interesting than I expected. Spoiler, without the numbers: the second predictor I reached for first didn't do what I assumed it would, and *why* it didn't is the most useful thing in this chapter.

## Picking up where the last model left off

Same dataset, same window, same model. `cell_data_sub` is `cell_data` restricted to DPI 3, 7 and 14, the stretch where a straight line is a defensible description of tissue loss, and the outcome is hemispheric tissue area. The area is `Tissue_Area`, in mm², the same column and the same units used throughout the book (the µm² duplicate is explained in @sec-eda-data-quality).

```{r}
#| label: tbl-multiple_data
#| tbl-cap: The DPI 3–14 subset, first rows

library(gt)
cell_data_sub <- subset(cell_data, DPI %in% c(3, 7, 14))
gt(head(cell_data_sub[, c("MouseID", "DPI", "Condition", "Tissue_Area", "Gfap_IntDen", "Pdgfrb_IntDen")]))
```

Before adding anything, let's refit the baseline, because everything that follows only means something in comparison to it. I'm keeping the `brms` defaults for priors, for the same reason as last chapter: I want the coefficients to reflect the data as directly as possible while we get the structure right, and @sec-priors-regularization is where we stop doing that on purpose.

```{r}
library(brms)

fit_dpi <- brm(
  Tissue_Area ~ DPI,
  data = cell_data_sub,
  seed = 123,
  file = "models/linear-regression-multiple_fit1.rds",
  file_refit = "never"
)
```

```{r}
summary(fit_dpi)
```

Same story as before: tissue area drops by about 0.67 units per day (95% credible interval roughly $-0.83$ to $-0.52$), and `sigma`, the typical distance between an animal and the line, sits around 1.85. Last chapter's posterior predictive check left us with a loose end: the model's single `sigma` was a compromise, too large for days 7 and 14 and too small for day 3, which is noticeably more spread out than the other two days. So here is the question this chapter keeps circling: can something *else we measured* absorb some of that leftover variation?

## A second predictor: does GFAP add anything?

If you were designing this study, I'd bet the first thing you'd reach for is GFAP. Reactive astrocytes wall off the infarct, GFAP is the marker for them, and they're the star of the whole dataset. It seems obvious that an animal with more GFAP signal has something different going on in its tissue than one with less.

`cell_data` gives us two GFAP measurements, and @sec-linear-regression-assumptions already told us we can't use both: `Gfap_Area` and `Gfap_IntDen` carried a VIF of about 50 together. I'm following that chapter's advice and keeping one. I chose `Gfap_IntDen` (integrated density, area weighted by intensity), because it captures both how much tissue is stained and how strongly, which is closer to "how much GFAP is there" than area alone. With `DPI` in the model, its VIF is only about 1.2, so the collinearity alarm from that chapter stays quiet.

One practical wrinkle: `Gfap_IntDen` runs from a few hundred to over a thousand, so a "one-unit" change is microscopic and the coefficient would be a tiny number nobody can read. I'll divide by 100, so a coefficient is the change in tissue area per 100 units of GFAP. That's a linear rescale: it changes the units of the coefficient and nothing else.

```{r}
cell_data_sub$Gfap_100 <- cell_data_sub$Gfap_IntDen / 100
cell_data_sub$DPI_f <- factor(cell_data_sub$DPI)  # for the per-day checks below
```

Now the part I want you to see in two steps, because the contrast is the point. First, GFAP *alone*, what most of us would do at the bench, plotting one marker against the outcome. Then GFAP together with `DPI`.

```{r}
fit_gfap_alone <- brm(
  Tissue_Area ~ Gfap_100,
  data = cell_data_sub,
  seed = 123,
  file = "models/linear-regression-multiple_fit2.rds",
  file_refit = "never"
)

fit_dpi_gfap <- brm(
  Tissue_Area ~ DPI + Gfap_100,
  data = cell_data_sub,
  seed = 123,
  file = "models/linear-regression-multiple_fit3.rds",
  file_refit = "never"
)
```

::: panel-tabset
### brms

```{r}
summary(fit_dpi_gfap)
```

The formula is the only thing that changed: `DPI + Gfap_100` gives every predictor its own slope, exactly the extension of @eq-linear-regression-multiple. Sampling is healthy (Rhat at 1.00, effective sample sizes well above 400, no divergences). The `DPI` slope barely moved from the baseline ($-0.68$, against $-0.67$ before). The `Gfap_100` slope is 0.05, with a 95% credible interval running from about $-0.21$ to $0.31$, comfortably on both sides of zero. `sigma` didn't shrink either (1.86, against 1.85): GFAP explained no extra variation.

### parsnip

```{r}
library(parsnip)
library(broom)

parsnip_dpi_gfap <- linear_reg() %>%
  set_engine("lm") %>%
  fit(Tissue_Area ~ DPI + Gfap_100, data = cell_data_sub)

tidy(parsnip_dpi_gfap, conf.int = TRUE)
```
:::

That's odd, isn't it? GFAP alone has a modest negative association with tissue area (Pearson's $r$ of about $-0.33$ in this subset, and a slope of $-0.40$ per 100 units whose interval barely reaches zero), and yet with `DPI` in the model it has nothing to add. Let me put both posteriors on the same axis, since the shift is the whole story.

Both posteriors are for a slope, and what I care about is where the mass sits relative to zero and how much the data moved it. A half-eye, instead of two bare intervals, shows the whole shape of each, which matters here because the "alone" posterior is wide and sits mostly, but not entirely, on one side of zero.

```{r}
#| label: fig-multiple_gfap_alone_vs_adjusted
#| fig-cap: Posterior for the GFAP slope on tissue area, alone versus adjusting for DPI
#| fig-width: 6.5
#| fig-height: 3.5

library(ggdist)
library(posterior)

gfap_slopes <- rbind(
  data.frame(model = "GFAP alone", slope = as_draws_df(fit_gfap_alone)$b_Gfap_100),
  data.frame(model = "GFAP, adjusting for DPI", slope = as_draws_df(fit_dpi_gfap)$b_Gfap_100)
)

ggplot(gfap_slopes, aes(x = slope, y = model, fill = model)) +
  stat_halfeye(.width = c(0.5, 0.95), point_interval = "median_qi") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", color = "grey40") +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("GFAP alone" = "#D55E00", "GFAP, adjusting for DPI" = "#0072B2")) +
  labs(x = "GFAP slope (change in tissue area per 100 units of Gfap_IntDen)", y = NULL) +
  Plot_theme +
  theme(legend.position = "none")
```

The orange posterior leans negative; the blue one is centered on zero and is about half as wide. Nothing about GFAP changed between the two fits. What changed is what we're asking. The reason is easiest to see in a picture of the raw data with the time points marked.

```{r}
#| label: fig-multiple_gfap_by_dpi
#| fig-cap: Tissue area against GFAP integrated density. The dashed line ignores DPI; the colored lines are fit within each day.
#| fig-width: 6.5
#| fig-height: 4.5
#| warning: false
#| message: false

dpi_cols <- c("3" = "#E69F00", "7" = "#009E73", "14" = "#CC79A7")

ggplot(cell_data_sub, aes(x = Gfap_100, y = Tissue_Area)) +
  geom_smooth(aes(group = 1), method = lm, se = FALSE,
              color = "black", linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_point(aes(color = factor(DPI, levels = c(3, 7, 14)),
                 shape = factor(DPI, levels = c(3, 7, 14))), size = 2.5) +
  geom_smooth(aes(color = factor(DPI, levels = c(3, 7, 14))),
              method = lm, se = FALSE) +
  scale_color_manual(values = dpi_cols) +
  labs(x = "GFAP integrated density (per 100 units)", y = "Tissue area",
       color = "DPI", shape = "DPI") +
  Plot_theme +
  theme(legend.position = "top")
```

Look at the three colored clouds separately. Within any one day, the line through the points is nearly flat: knowing an animal's GFAP tells you almost nothing about its tissue area *once you know how many days it has been since the ischemia*. The dashed line looks like a relationship only because both variables travel with time: GFAP climbs from day 3 to day 7 and stays high, and tissue area falls over the same period. GFAP was tagging along with `DPI`, and the marginal slope was borrowing `DPI`'s effect.

### What "adjusting" actually means

You will read, in nearly every methods section, that a coefficient is the effect of a predictor "holding the others constant". That phrase is a little too generous. @gelman2020 point out that a regression coefficient is a comparison between *different* animals, not an experiment on one: `Gfap_100`'s coefficient compares the average outcome of animals that differ by one unit of GFAP but share the same `DPI`. And @mcelreath2020 puts it in the framing this book has been using since @sec-linear-regression-what: each coefficient answers, "what is the value of knowing this predictor, after I already know all the others?" For GFAP, once I know the day, the answer is "very little".

::: callout-tip
### A note on causality, before it bites

Adjusting for a variable makes a *predictive* statement, not automatically a causal one. @mcelreath2020 is blunt about two ways the arrow can go wrong: controlling for a variable that sits *downstream* of what you're studying (post-treatment bias) can erase a real effect, and controlling for a common consequence of two variables (a collider) can manufacture a relationship that isn't there. Statistical fit can't tell you which variable is a good control and which is a bad one; that takes a causal story drawn *outside* the model. Here, DPI is a design variable set by the experimenter, so adjusting for it is uncontroversial, but I'm not claiming GFAP "has no effect" on tissue area, only that it carries no *additional* predictive information beyond time. We'll draw those causal diagrams properly in @sec-causal-inference-splines.
:::

::: callout-tip
### The feature-engineering seed from last time

@sec-linear-regression-assumptions left open the idea of building a composite variable out of a correlated pair instead of discarding one [@kuhn2021]. That's a good move when the redundant pair carries signal worth preserving. Here, the discarded `Gfap_Area` had nothing extra to say either, and a composite of two quantities that add nothing beyond `DPI` isn't going to rescue them. I'll leave composites for a chapter where the raw pair earns its keep.
:::

## A categorical predictor: DPI as a set of days

So far I've treated `DPI` as a number, so the model assumes each extra day costs the same amount of tissue. But we only sampled three days. What if I stop assuming a straight line and just let each day have its own mean?

That is exactly what a categorical predictor does. Turn `DPI` into a factor, and the model estimates one mean per day, with day 3 as the baseline (the intercept) and each other day reported as a difference from it. It's the same linear model machinery, only with indicator variables instead of a slope, which is why a t-test or an ANOVA turns out to be a special case, as @sec-linear-regression-what noted.

The reason to do this here is as a check on the linearity claim from last chapter: if a straight line is honest, the per-day means should fall close to it.

```{r}
fit_dpi_factor <- brm(
  Tissue_Area ~ DPI_f,
  data = cell_data_sub,
  seed = 123,
  file = "models/linear-regression-multiple_fit4.rds",
  file_refit = "never"
)
```

::: panel-tabset
### brms

```{r}
summary(fit_dpi_factor)
```

### parsnip

```{r}
parsnip_dpi_factor <- linear_reg() %>%
  set_engine("lm") %>%
  fit(Tissue_Area ~ DPI_f, data = cell_data_sub)

tidy(parsnip_dpi_factor, conf.int = TRUE)
```
:::

The `Intercept` is the mean tissue area at day 3 (about 16.9). `DPI_f7` and `DPI_f14` are how far day 7 and day 14 sit below it: roughly 3.0 and 7.5 units. Notice that `DPI_f7` is a *difference from day 3*, not from zero, which is the most common misreading of dummy coding.

Now the linearity check itself. I'll draw the straight-line posterior as a graded ribbon, and lay the three per-day means on top with their intervals.

```{r}
#| label: fig-multiple_linear_vs_factor
#| fig-cap: Straight-line fit (ribbon) versus a separate mean for each day (points and intervals)
#| fig-width: 6.5
#| fig-height: 4
#| warning: false

epred_long <- function(fit, newdata, ndraws = 500) {
  ep <- posterior_epred(fit, newdata = newdata, ndraws = ndraws)
  data.frame(
    draw = rep(seq_len(nrow(ep)), times = ncol(ep)),
    row = rep(seq_len(ncol(ep)), each = nrow(ep)),
    y = as.vector(ep)
  )
}

grid_line <- data.frame(DPI = seq(3, 14, length.out = 40))
line_draws <- epred_long(fit_dpi, grid_line)
line_draws$DPI <- grid_line$DPI[line_draws$row]

grid_fac <- data.frame(DPI_f = factor(c(3, 7, 14)))
fac_draws <- epred_long(fit_dpi_factor, grid_fac)
fac_draws$DPI <- as.numeric(as.character(grid_fac$DPI_f[fac_draws$row]))

ggplot() +
  stat_lineribbon(data = line_draws, aes(x = DPI, y = y, fill_ramp = after_stat(level)),
                  .width = c(0.5, 0.8, 0.95), fill = "#0072B2") +
  stat_pointinterval(data = fac_draws, aes(x = DPI, y = y),
                     color = "#D55E00", point_size = 3, .width = 0.95,
                     position = position_nudge(x = 0.15)) +
  geom_point(data = cell_data_sub, aes(x = DPI, y = Tissue_Area),
             color = "grey30", alpha = 0.5, size = 1.5) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = c(3, 7, 14)) +
  labs(x = "Days post-ischemia (DPI)", y = "Tissue area") +
  Plot_theme
```

The orange means sit inside the blue band at all three days, so a straight line is a fair summary of these three groups. The categorical model isn't a rival to the linear one. It's a way of checking it. (The price of the categorical version is one extra parameter, and it can't say anything about days we didn't sample.)

## Interactions: does GFAP's story change over time?

Here I have to confess a change of plan. The natural experiment in this dataset looks like `Condition` (sham versus MCAO) crossed with `DPI`: does the *trajectory* of tissue area over time differ between the two? It's the question I wanted to ask. But it can't be answered with these data, and it's worth seeing why, because it's a design lesson before it's a statistical one.

::: callout-warning
### Why `Condition * DPI` is not estimable here

Sham animals exist only at DPI 0 (n = 7). MCAO animals exist only at DPI 3, 7, 14 and 30. `Condition` and "DPI = 0" are the same variable: there is no sham animal at any later day and no MCAO animal at day 0. An interaction asks whether the difference between conditions *changes* with time, which requires observing both conditions at more than one time. No model can conjure the missing cells; a formula like `DPI * Condition` would be fit on paper and identified by nothing. This is a question to settle at the design stage (sham animals at every time point), not to rescue in the analysis.
:::

What I *can* ask is a real interaction question with the data in hand. Last section GFAP had no additional association with tissue area, averaged across days. But the biology of reactive gliosis is not the same at day 3 as at day 14. Perhaps the relationship between GFAP and tissue changes with time even though its average is flat. Formally, that's an interaction: the slope of one predictor depends on the value of another.

$$
\text{Area}_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1 \text{DPI}_i + \beta_2 \text{GFAP}_i + \beta_3 (\text{DPI}_i \times \text{GFAP}_i) + \epsilon_i
$$ {#eq-multiple-interaction}

$\beta_3$ is the new piece: how much the GFAP slope changes for each additional day. If $\beta_3$ is zero, the GFAP slope is the same at every time point.

One thing to fix before fitting. With an interaction, $\beta_1$ and $\beta_2$ stop meaning "the effect of that predictor" and start meaning "the effect *when the other predictor is zero*". A GFAP of zero and a DPI of zero are both outside the observed range, so I'd be interpreting coefficients at a place no animal lives. Centering solves it: I'll center DPI at day 7 (the middle day) and GFAP at its sample mean, so the main effects become the effect at a typical animal.

```{r}
cell_data_sub$DPI_c <- cell_data_sub$DPI - 7
cell_data_sub$Gfap_c <- cell_data_sub$Gfap_100 - mean(cell_data_sub$Gfap_100)

fit_interaction <- brm(
  Tissue_Area ~ DPI_c * Gfap_c,
  data = cell_data_sub,
  seed = 123,
  file = "models/linear-regression-multiple_fit5.rds",
  file_refit = "never"
)
```

::: panel-tabset
### brms

```{r}
summary(fit_interaction)
```

`DPI_c * Gfap_c` expands to both main effects plus their product, `DPI_c:Gfap_c`, which is $\beta_3$. Its posterior median is 0.01 per day, with a 95% credible interval from about $-0.06$ to $0.07$: small, and on both sides of zero.

### parsnip

```{r}
parsnip_interaction <- linear_reg() %>%
  set_engine("lm") %>%
  fit(Tissue_Area ~ DPI_c * Gfap_c, data = cell_data_sub)

tidy(parsnip_interaction, conf.int = TRUE)
```
:::

A single number for an interaction is hard to feel, so I'll draw what it implies: the fitted GFAP relationship on each day, with its uncertainty. I'm restricting each panel to the range of GFAP actually observed on that day, so we're not extrapolating a line to places with no animals in them. The graded band shows the 50%, 80% and 95% credible levels, so a reader sees a spectrum of plausibility instead of one hard edge.

```{r}
#| label: fig-multiple_interaction_by_day
#| fig-cap: Fitted GFAP–tissue area relationship on each day, from the interaction model
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 3.5
#| warning: false

grid_int <- do.call(rbind, lapply(c(3, 7, 14), function(dp) {
  g <- cell_data_sub$Gfap_c[cell_data_sub$DPI == dp]
  data.frame(DPI = dp, DPI_c = dp - 7, Gfap_c = seq(min(g), max(g), length.out = 30))
}))

int_draws <- epred_long(fit_interaction, grid_int)
int_draws$DPI <- grid_int$DPI[int_draws$row]
int_draws$Gfap_100 <- grid_int$Gfap_c[int_draws$row] + mean(cell_data_sub$Gfap_100)

ggplot(int_draws, aes(x = Gfap_100, y = y)) +
  stat_lineribbon(aes(fill_ramp = after_stat(level)), .width = c(0.5, 0.8, 0.95), fill = "#0072B2") +
  geom_point(data = cell_data_sub, aes(y = Tissue_Area),
             color = "grey30", alpha = 0.6, size = 1.5) +
  facet_wrap(~DPI, labeller = label_both, scales = "free_x") +
  scale_x_continuous(n.breaks = 4) +
  labs(x = "GFAP integrated density (per 100 units)", y = "Tissue area",
       fill_ramp = "Credible level") +
  Plot_theme
```

The three fitted lines are close to flat and close to each other: the implied GFAP slope is about $-0.01$ on day 3, 0.03 on day 7 and 0.10 on day 14 (per 100 units), each with a 95% interval spanning roughly half a unit on either side of zero. A flat line, or one tilting either way, fits inside every panel. What the data can support is modest: **no reliable evidence that GFAP's association with tissue area changes over time**, with only 31 animals and only 8 to 12 per day. Reporting that plainly, instead of hunting for the interaction that looks best, is the point.

## Transformations: when a log helps, and when it doesn't

@sec-linear-regression-assumptions quoted Inchausti's caution about "esoteric transformations" [@inchausti2023], and I stand by it as a default. But a caution isn't a ban, and a log is the one transformation that has a real biological rationale for a predictor like `Gfap_IntDen`: it's an intensity times an area, positive, and plausibly multiplicative, so a doubling may matter more than a fixed increment. If `Gfap_IntDen` is right-skewed, a log-scale might describe it, and its relationship to the outcome, better.

I don't want to decide that from memory. Here is the predictor on its original and log2 scales side by side. I use log base 2 rather than the natural log because a unit on that scale reads as "a doubling", which is easier to communicate at the bench.

```{r}
#| label: fig-multiple_log_hist
#| fig-cap: Distribution of GFAP integrated density, original and log2 scale
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 3.2

library(patchwork)

cell_data_sub$Gfap_log2 <- log2(cell_data_sub$Gfap_IntDen)

skew <- function(x) mean((x - mean(x))^3) / sd(x)^3

p_raw <- ggplot(cell_data_sub, aes(x = Gfap_IntDen)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 12, fill = "#0072B2", color = "white", alpha = 0.85) +
  labs(x = "Gfap_IntDen", y = "Count") +
  Plot_theme

p_log <- ggplot(cell_data_sub, aes(x = Gfap_log2)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 12, fill = "#0072B2", color = "white", alpha = 0.85) +
  labs(x = "log2(Gfap_IntDen)", y = "Count") +
  Plot_theme

p_raw + p_log
```

Skewness is about `r round(skew(cell_data_sub$Gfap_IntDen), 2)` on the original scale and `r round(skew(cell_data_sub$Gfap_log2), 2)` on the log2 scale: a mild right tail that the log does flatten out, but not the kind of skew that by itself demands a fix. A tidier histogram isn't the goal, though. Whether the log helps the *model* is the actual question, so let's fit it and compare.

```{r}
fit_log <- brm(
  Tissue_Area ~ DPI + Gfap_log2,
  data = cell_data_sub,
  seed = 123,
  file = "models/linear-regression-multiple_fit6.rds",
  file_refit = "never"
)
```

::: panel-tabset
### brms

```{r}
summary(fit_log)
```

### parsnip

```{r}
parsnip_log <- linear_reg() %>%
  set_engine("lm") %>%
  fit(Tissue_Area ~ DPI + Gfap_log2, data = cell_data_sub)

tidy(parsnip_log, conf.int = TRUE)
```
:::

Reading the log-scale coefficient takes a translation: `Gfap_log2` is the change in tissue area per *doubling* of GFAP, not per 100 units. The estimate is 0.26 units per doubling, with a 95% credible interval from about $-0.84$ to 1.42. The `DPI` slope is essentially unchanged ($-0.69$), GFAP is still indistinguishable from zero, and the residual `sigma` hasn't budged (1.86). The transformation bought a tidier predictor and nothing in the model's fit, at the cost of a coefficient that needs a paragraph to explain. Which is what the guidance from last time predicts: the log earns its keep when the biology is multiplicative and the fit improves, and neither is true here. So the linear-scale model stands.

::: callout-tip
### Rescaling is not transforming

Dividing GFAP by 100, or centering DPI at day 7, are linear changes: they shift and stretch the axis but leave the shape of the relationship alone, so the fit is identical and only the meaning of the coefficients moves. A log changes the *shape*, which is why it needs justification and rescaling doesn't.
:::

## Can we trust the sampling?

Before I lean on any of these fits, a housekeeping check I have only done informally so far. `summary()` shows Rhat and the effective sample sizes, but one model at a time, and I have quoted them for only some of the six. A single table across every model in the chapter is cheaper than trusting my eye six times, and it uses the same thresholds as @sec-mcmc-model-checking: Rhat below 1.01, both effective sample sizes above 400, and zero divergent transitions.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-multiple_mcmc
#| tbl-cap: MCMC diagnostics for every model fitted in this chapter

source("functions/mcmc_check.R")

multiple_checks <- mcmc_check(list(
  "DPI" = fit_dpi,
  "GFAP alone" = fit_gfap_alone,
  "DPI + GFAP" = fit_dpi_gfap,
  "DPI (categorical)" = fit_dpi_factor,
  "DPI x GFAP" = fit_interaction,
  "DPI + log2 GFAP" = fit_log
))
stopifnot(all(multiple_checks$ok))

gt(multiple_checks) |>
  fmt_number(columns = max_rhat, decimals = 3) |>
  fmt_number(columns = c(min_ess_bulk, min_ess_tail), decimals = 0)
```

All six fits clear the bar: the worst Rhat is `r sprintf("%.3f", max(multiple_checks$max_rhat))`, the smallest effective sample size is `r round(min(multiple_checks$min_ess_bulk, multiple_checks$min_ess_tail))`, and there are `r sum(multiple_checks$divergences)` divergent transitions in total. That settles the sampling side; whether the *models* describe the biology is the next question.

## Does this model's story match the data?

The GFAP model is not the one I'd take forward as the best description of tissue area (the baseline says the same with fewer parameters), but it is the natural place to run the check that started the chapter. The question was whether a second predictor could absorb the day-3 spread that left the single-predictor model's predictive check with a second hump. @sec-mcmc-model-checking gives us `pp_check()` for the overall shape, and a grouped version lets us look at the day-3 spread directly.

```{r}
#| label: fig-multiple_ppcheck
#| fig-cap: Posterior predictive check for the DPI + GFAP model
#| fig-width: 6
#| fig-height: 4

pp_check(fit_dpi_gfap, ndraws = 50)
```

The overall picture is close to last chapter's: replicates bracket the data roughly, but the observed density (dark line) has two distinct humps, around 10 and 14, while nearly every replicate is a single smooth mound. That's not surprising now. GFAP added nothing, so it couldn't fix anything. To look at the specific problem, I'll compare the standard deviation of the observed data on each day with the standard deviation in replicated datasets.

```{r}
#| label: fig-multiple_ppcheck_sd
#| fig-cap: Observed standard deviation of tissue area on each day (dark line) against replicates from the DPI + GFAP model
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 3.5
#| message: false

library(bayesplot)

# brms only stores the variables in the formula, so we hand bayesplot the
# grouping variable ourselves (rows are in the same order as the model's data)
ppc_stat_grouped(
  y = cell_data_sub$Tissue_Area,
  yrep = posterior_predict(fit_dpi_gfap, ndraws = 500),
  group = cell_data_sub$DPI_f,
  stat = "sd"
)
```

Each panel asks the same question: is the spread we actually saw on that day (the dark bar) the sort of spread this model would produce? On day 3 it isn't. The observed standard deviation is about 3.1, far out in the right tail of what the model simulates (typically around 1.5 to 2). Days 7 and 14 go the other way: the observed spread, about 1.0, sits at the low edge of their replicates. A single `sigma` for all three days is a compromise: too small for day 3, too large for days 7 and 14. (Part of day 3's spread is one animal with a tissue area near 10.5 while its neighbors sit above 15; @fig-multiple_linear_vs_factor shows it. With eight animals in that group, one unusual animal moves the standard deviation a lot.) No predictor we've added addresses this, because the trouble isn't in the *mean*, it's in the *variance*.

A last question we can answer honestly: does adding any of these predictors improve out-of-sample prediction? Leave-one-out cross-validation compares candidates on held-out data. It is a relative judgment, not an absolute one, so it never replaces the checks above.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-multiple_loo
#| tbl-cap: Leave-one-out comparison of the candidate models (differences are relative to the best-ranked model)
#| warning: false

loo_tab <- loo_compare(list(
  `DPI` = loo(fit_dpi),
  `DPI + GFAP` = loo(fit_dpi_gfap),
  `DPI (categorical)` = loo(fit_dpi_factor),
  `DPI x GFAP` = loo(fit_interaction)
))

gt(data.frame(model = rownames(loo_tab), round(loo_tab[, 1:2], 2)))
```

The simplest model, tissue area as a straight-line function of days, ranks first. `DPI + GFAP` trails it by about half a unit of expected log predictive density (`elpd_diff`), with a standard error bigger than the gap, so those two are indistinguishable. The categorical and interaction models trail by roughly two units, a small but consistent price for extra parameters that bought nothing. (One animal has a Pareto-$k$ above 0.7 in every model, meaning its leave-one-out estimate is less reliable than the rest; with the ranking this clear, I won't chase it.) That's an anticlimax only if you expected a winner. Adding parameters is only worth it when they buy something, and here none of them did.

The variance problem is real and unsolved. The fix is to model `sigma` itself as a function of the predictor, and @sec-multivariate-distributional-regression does that. Until then, I'd treat every interval in this chapter as slightly optimistic for day 3.

::: callout-tip
### Frequentist equivalent

Every `parsnip` table above lands close to its `brms` counterpart (the Bayesian intervals run a touch wider, since they also carry the uncertainty in `sigma`), for the reason @sec-linear-regression-single-continuous gave: with 31 animals the likelihood is far sharper than a default, nearly flat prior (or even a weak informative one), so the posterior is shaped almost entirely by it, which is what `lm` maximizes on its own [@gelman2020]. The two approaches would start to disagree where the data are thin relative to the model. With 31 animals, an interaction model spends four parameters, and a weakly informative prior would pull an unstable interaction estimate toward zero where `lm` reports it at face value. Here the interaction is small either way, so there's nothing for the prior to rescue, but it's the place to look if you ever fit a richer model to fewer animals.
:::

## Where this leaves us

A second predictor turned out to be a lesson in reading coefficients rather than a better model. GFAP looked related to tissue loss until we asked what it added once we knew the day; the answer was nothing, because both had been moving with time. A categorical `DPI` confirmed the straight line was fair. The interaction we could actually fit was small and uncertain, and the one I wanted (`Condition * DPI`) turned out to be a design question that no analysis could rescue. A log transformation earned nothing. And the variance problem from the last chapter is still with us, now a bit more precisely located.

Next, @sec-glm-intro steps outside the Gaussian world entirely. Everything so far assumed an outcome that can, in principle, take any real value. Many of the outcomes neuroscientists care about (did the animal respond, how many spikes fired) can't, and the linear model needs a new set of clothes to handle them.
